items.title: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality
items.summary: Too many websites look alike. They use familiar layouts, repeat the same patterns, and often leave little impression once you’ve moved on. Andy Clarke explores how understanding a company’s story can lead to more distinctive designs, using modular and compound grids to create layouts with character. Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.titleJa: Beyond 12 Columns: Designing Layouts With Personality
items.summaryJa: レイアウトはただ記事を並べるだけでなく、企業の個性や伝えたいメッセージを反映させるべきだと筆者は主張している。十二列グリッドに頼るだけでなく、四方形のモジュールを組み合わせたモジュラー/gridを用い、ヒエラルキーや空白の扱いを工夫することで Wheelman のような独自性を表現できると説明している。さらに、複数のグリッドを組み合わせたコンパウンドグリッドを活用すれば、雑誌・ショップ・サービスといった異なる目的を持つページでも予測可能さを避け、読みやすさと個性を両立できると述べている。

items.titleJa: Claude Codeのeffortでトークン量はどれくらい変わるか検証してみた
items.summaryJa: Claude Codeのeffort設定（low・medium・high・xhigh・max）を変えて同じ課題を実行し、出力トークン量・時間・換算コストを測定した報告。結果として、mediumからhighへ1段階上げると出力トークンはモデル全体で1.2〜1.3倍、xhighへ上げると2.3〜2.4倍増加する一方、lowではOpus 5.5とFable 5.2で約3割減、Sonnet 5.5はほぼ変動なし。 thinkingトークンやツール呼び出し回数、入力トークン等も増減に連動し、特に少し重い課題や複数ファイルにまたがる機能追加で差が顕著だった。全4課題の中では、どのモデル・effortでも隠しテストはすべて合格し、品質差は測定時点では顕著でないとの結論。低コスト志向なら低めのeffort、確認重視ならhigh程度を検討、xhighは2倍以上のトークン増となるため慎重な判断が推奨されています。

items.titleJa: Claude Opus 5.5とFable 5.2はどちらを使うべきか、Claude Codeで同じ課題を解かせて比べてみた
items.summaryJa: Opus 5.5とFable 5.2を同じ課題で比較した結果、4つの課題では両モデルとも全問合格で差はほとんど出ませんでした。出力トークンと時間を同じeffortで比べると、Fable 5.2は約1.1～1.3倍のトークン量と時間、換算コストは約2.1～2.5倍と高くなり、同じコストで使うにはOpus 5.5が有利です。ただし、知識系の質問やバグ修正など一部課題ではFable 5.2の方がトークン量・時間が少なくなる場面もあり、課題の内容次第で使い分けが推奨されています。

items.titleJa: CVE-2026-98432（Linuxカーネル IPv4 TCPのuse-after-free）各ディストリビューションの対応状況【2026年11月10日時点】
items.summaryJa: CVE-2026-98432の対策として、各ディストリビューションの現行サポート版はほぼ修正版が公開済みである。Debian、RHEL8/9/10と互換ディストリ、SLES、Amazon Linux、Ubuntu 22.04/24.04/26.04/26.10には修正カーネルが提供され、Ubuntuはpocketによって状況が異なる。24.04は-updatesのみのケースもあり、26.04/22.04は-security入り、20.04/18.04/16.04標準カーネルやSUSEリアルタイム系・RHEL AI 3などは未修正または作業中の項目が残る。脆弱性概要はIPv4 TCPの接続確立処理におけるinet_opt/ireq_optの解放をRCU猶予期間待ちなしで行っていたこと、CVEは2026年10月15日公表、修正は上流で10月5日。悪用報告として認証なしでroot実行を示す公開情報がある一方、公式の広範な悪用証拠は未確認。上流修正系列のUTLは7.3/7.2/6.18/6.12/6.6/6.1/5.15/5.10等で提供済み、4.4–5.4は上流で修正なし。各ディストリビューションの個別状況は、Debianはtrixie/bookworm/ELTSで修正済み、Ubuntuは26.10/26.04/24.04/22.04/20.04で修正状況が異なり、RHEL系はリリースごとに修正済みのカーネルが提供され、SLES/Amazon Linux/Oracle Linux/AlmaLinux/Rockyなども修正済み。注意点として、USNやLTSの適用口実、HWE/クラウド向けのカーネルでは適用状況が異なる場合があるため、実環境では各ベンダーの公式情報を確認する必要がある。

items.title: Decision models take 26% of requests; Anthropic now wins new teams 2:1
items.summary: AI Gateway Production Index — November 2026 Every month, AI Gateway routes more than 100 trillion tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage looks like in today’s enterprise and startup landscape across language, decision, voice, image, and video models. We publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from August , September , and October . November 2026 Summary In six weeks, decision models grew to one in four gateway requests, while accounting for half a cent of every dollar spent. Close to a third of all paid teams used one in October. Among teams processing over 10 billion tokens a month, seven in ten used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a voice model in October, up from 4% in July. OpenAI and Anthropic now reach about the same share of paid teams, and new teams in October picked Anthropic nearly two to one . OpenAI’s share of gateway spend, meanwhile, is up by two-thirds since December. More than half of language-model requests went to models less than two months old, up from less than three in ten. Within one month of a typical model’s peak usage, three in four of the teams using it have moved on. Decision models account for 26% of all requests Production AI is splitting into two jobs: generation and judgment. Until recently, when software needed to make a quick call, a team could use either a fixed rule that was cheap but rigid, or a language model that was smart but slow and expensive. Decision models are now a third option. They classify, score, or pick between choices instead of generating text, and cost about a seventieth as much per request as a language model. They arrived on AI Gateway in mid-September, and there are now 15 decision models available from eight different vendors. In October, nearly a third of paid teams on AI Gateway used a decision model. About 11% of paid teams used a decision model without sending a single request to a text-generating model. Decision models cost far less per token and give very short answers, so even though they received about one in four gateway requests in October, they accounted for just 0.53% of total spend. Almost all of that request volume went to Jev from TypeSafe AI, which alone received nearly four times Anthropic’s total requests. For every $1 teams spent on Jev, they spent $64 on Anthropic models. Decision models are most common among the teams that run the most AI. Just over one in five teams running fewer than 10 million tokens used a decision model in October. At 100 million to 1 billion tokens, nearly half used one. Above 10 billion, seven in ten did. This is partly because big teams use more of everything. The top 1% of teams by spend use a median of 29 different models, and the bottom tenth use only one. It’s also volume. The more requests a team sends, the more it has to gain from a model that makes simple decisions faster and far more cost-effectively. Voice adoption is up 2.6x since July About one in nine paid teams used a voice model in October, up from one in 24 in July, an increase of 161%. New teams are using voice, and existing teams are adding it. Among teams that paid in both July and October, the share using voice went from 5% to 14%. Teams that use voice are also using more of it. The share of teams sending at least 100 voice requests a month grew fivefold, and six in ten of September’s voice teams returned in October, up from fewer than half in July. A spoken conversation with an AI app takes three steps: A voice model turns the user’s speech into text A language model writes the reply Another voice model reads the reply back to the user Most voice teams use just one or two of these pieces. Use of speech-to-text models has nearly tripled since July, and text-to-speech has more than tripled. Some models do all three steps on their own. In July, about a quarter of voice teams used one of these all-in-one models, and one in six assembled the pieces themselves. By October, those numbers had swapped. For most teams, voice is a new way for users to talk to an app or agent they already have. Teams’ preferred language models stay in the middle, and they can add voice at one end or both. Anthropic wins new teams two to one, and OpenAI’s share of spend is up two-thirds Last December, 70 of every 100 paid teams on AI Gateway used an OpenAI model and 48 used an Anthropic model. By October, the two labs were nearly level, with OpenAI at 55 and Anthropic at 54. Both labs now reach more of the teams that have been on the gateway since December, but Anthropic’s reach grew more. The share of these teams using Anthropic rose from about half to two-thirds, while OpenAI’s rose from about three in four to four in five. Most of Anthropic’s gain came from new teams. In October, it was the first-choice lab for nearly twice as many of them as OpenAI. But among the biggest teams, both labs already have nearly everyone. More than nine in ten of the top 1% by spend use both Anthropic and OpenAI. With these teams, the labs now compete for how much of the work each one gets. On that measure, Anthropic still leads, but OpenAI has gained ground. OpenAI now takes nearly 15 cents of every dollar spent on the gateway, up from about 9 in December, while Anthropic’s halved to about 32 cents over the same period. Most AI traffic now runs on models less than two months old Teams are moving to new models almost as fast as labs release them. More than half of October’s language-model requests went to models less than 60 days old. Before September, that share had never passed three in ten. Within each model family, a new version arrives every 61 days at the median, and a typical model peaks within a month of launch. Four weeks later, three in four of the teams using it at its peak aren’t using it anymore, whether or not a successor has shipped in the family. Most of those teams are still on AI Gateway, using other models. Teams switch models frequently, usually to something newer, and often to another lab. In October, about half of teams running at least 10 million tokens a month changed their most-used model. Four in five of those moved to a more recent release, and six in ten moved to a different lab. Older models stay in use, often alongside a newer primary model. Seven in ten teams running at least 10 million tokens a month still used a model at least ten months old in October, but for the typical team it ran less than 3% of its tokens. AI models now have a half-life of about six weeks. That means that, to the teams using them, labs are only as good as their latest model and have to re-earn their business with every new one. Also in October’s data Opus 5.5 was the top model by spend in its first full month. It took about one in seven dollars across all teams. Four of the six most widely used models on AI Gateway are Anthropic’s: Sonnet 5.5 (reaching 26% of paid teams), Haiku 5.5 (22%), Haiku 4.5 (20%), and Opus 5.5 (18%). Jev (28%) and GPT-6 Luna (19%) are the other two. Image and video both had their biggest month yet on AI Gateway. More teams than ever are putting spend on them, and the largest teams are adopting them the fastest. About a third of the top 1% of teams by spend now use an image model, up from a quarter in July. One in six use a video model, up from one in ten. OpenAI’s newest image model, GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, took the lead in image spend in its first full month, followed by its Flare and GPT-Image-2 models. ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 led video spend for a third month running, ahead of Google’s Veo 3.1 and Kuaishou’s Kling 3.0. About this data This report uses anonymized, aggregate traffic routed through Vercel AI Gateway through October 2026. A few notes on measurement: Spend is estimated at published list prices; actual bills may differ. Paid teams are teams with at least one paid request in the month. Team size is measured by a team’s total tokens that month. Decision models are the models classified as decision models in the AI Gateway model list. Each model version is counted separately. A model’s age is measured from that version’s first day on AI Gateway, and gateway history begins October 20, 2025. Switching rates compare paid teams with at least 10 million tokens in both September and October. A team’s most-used model is measured by tokens. Voice figures begin June 22, 2026. Teams that “assembled the pieces” used speech-to-text, a language model, and text-to-speech on the same day. A new team’s first-choice lab is the lab it sent the most language-model requests to in its first month. All figures use the most recent data and protocol available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated. Read more about our methodology , and explore or download the public data .
